## make a simple regression model
Numerical~Numerical helper file used for this.

```{r}
bears <- read.csv(file="BEARS.csv",header = TRUE)
#adjust factors to be factors
bears$SEX<- as.factor(bears$SEX)
bears$MONTH<- as.factor(bears$MONTH)
```

## Model LENGTH ~ NECK  this is an example  
```{r}
plot(LENGTH~NECK,data=bears)
```

As neck circumference increases, length tends to increase. The plot is primarily linear.

```{r}
model.1 <- lm(LENGTH~NECK,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.1)
```
The adjusted R-Squared is 0.7476. 

Compare all models that predict LENGTH other than NECK.  
Then order them from worst to best by its value of Adjusted-R squared (bigger is better), or by RSE (residual standard error) where smaller is better.

I'll conduct a final ranking at the end of this whole thing.

## Model LENGTH ~ HEADLEN
```{r}
plot(LENGTH~HEADLEN,data=bears)
```
As head length increases, so does length. However, this plot is not entirely linear and has some slight deviation.

```{r}
model.2 <- lm(LENGTH~HEADLEN,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.2)
```
The adjusted R-Squared is 0.8434, bigger than the previous model's... wowee!

## Model LENGTH ~ HeadWTH

```{r}
plot(LENGTH~HEADWTH,data=bears)
```
This is kind of a weird plot... It appears that as Head width increases, length loosely increases as well. However there is quite a bit of deviation from the usual linear plot.

```{r}
model.3 <- lm(LENGTH~HEADWTH,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.3)
```
The adjusted R-Squared is 0.5321, much lower than the previous ones. This makes this plot the lowest score so far.
## Model LENGTH ~ CHEST

```{r}
plot(LENGTH~CHEST,data=bears)
```
Fairly similar to the first two plots; as chest size increases so does the length in a somewhat linear fashion. There is a bit of deviation as well.
```{r}
model.4 <- lm(LENGTH~CHEST,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.4)
```
The adjusted R-Squared is 0.7869, making it the second largest so far.

## Model LENGTH ~ WEIGHT

```{r}
plot(LENGTH~WEIGHT,data=bears)
```
As weight increases, length does as well, especially at the beginning of the plot. This makes the beginning of the plot deviate a bit from the usual linear plot...
```{r}
model.5 <- lm(LENGTH~WEIGHT,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.5)
```
